stories.title: YTL Power scrutinised amid Nvidia turmoil, alleged China links
stories.summary: YTL Power International experienced its steepest weekly share decline in nearly two years as investor anxiety mounted over the Malaysian utility's alleged connections to Chinese-linked entities amid the broader Nvidia chip diversion controversy. The selloff reflects market uncertainty about whether YTL's data center partnerships and GPU procurement activities could face regulatory or reputational fallout.
stories.why_it_matters: YTL's share price trauma demonstrates how quickly Malaysia's data center investment narrative has shifted from unalloyed enthusiasm to risk-averse scrutiny; even unproven allegations of China ties now trigger capital flight. For Malaysian policymakers, the episode underscores the urgency of clarifying ownership structures and chip import audit trails before foreign investors broadly reprice Malaysian digital infrastructure risk; for YTL specifically, restoring confidence requires unprecedented transparency about its GPU supply chain partners and ultimate end-customers.

stories.title_zh: YTL Power在NVIDIA动荡和 alleged 中国关联指控中受到审视
stories.summary_zh: YTL Power International经历了近两年最陡峭的周度股价下跌，因为投资者对其 alleged 与中国关联实体的联系在更广泛的Nvidia芯片转移争议中日益焦虑。该抛售反映了市场对YTL的数据中心合作伙伴关系和GPU采购活动是否可能面临监管或声誉 fallout 的不确定性。
stories.why_zh: YTL的股价创伤展示了马来西亚数据中心投资叙事如何从纯粹热情迅速转向风险规避审查；即使是未经证实的中国关联指控现在也会触发资本 flight。对马来西亚政策制定者而言，该事件凸显了在外国投资者广泛重新定价马来西亚数字基础设施风险之前，澄清所有权结构和芯片进口审计 trail 的紧迫性；对YTL specifically，恢复信心需要对其GPU供应链合作伙伴和最终终端客户前所未有的透明度。
stories.content:
(Nov 16): YTL Power International Bhd (KL:YTLPOWR) shares took a breather Monday after their worst weekly selloff in nearly two years as turmoil surrounding Nvidia Corp and allegations the Malaysian utility has links to Chinese-connected firms cast a shadow over its artificial intelligence business.

The utility firm’s shares plunged 13% last week, the steepest weekly decline since January 2025, erasing more than RM3 billion (US$733 million) in market value. Intensifying scrutiny over Nvidia following Jensen Huang’s ouster as chief executive over reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy, has weighed on YTL.

Adding to concerns, spy-themed short seller Culper Research alleged in a May report that Megaspeed International — the Singapore-based cloud firm at the centre of the Nvidia controversy — is a major YTL customer. Citing a Megaspeed employee, Culper claimed YTL sought to keep the relationship private as it supplied Nvidia chips to Chinese customers including Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.

YTL and Megaspeed haven’t publicly confirmed such a relationship, and Culper’s claims haven’t been independently verified.

YTL Power and parent YTL Corp Bhd (KL:YTL) didn’t respond to requests for comment. Megaspeed didn’t respond to requests for comment.

In a Monday research note, MBSB Research analyst Royce Tan said there is no credible evidence implicating YTL Power for alleged chip diversion, but added that a formal clarification from the utility would address uncertainties.

“We believe it is important to distinguish the allegations surrounding Nvidia and Megaspeed from YTL Power’s own operations, which is mainly a co-location model where it provides space, power and cooling to third-party tenants rather than directly operating GPU computing infrastructure,” Tan wrote.

MBSB maintained its YTL "buy" recommendation.

YTL Power was up about 3% Monday and is currently valued at RM39 billion. Parent YTL Corp gained 1% Monday after a 10% weekly slump last week.

YTL Power partnered with Nvidia in 2023 for a RM20 billion artificial intelligence data centre project in Malaysia, helping propel its shares to record highs. The facility in Johor state began operating in October 2025, running Nvidia’s Grace Blackwell chips.

Malaysia said it’s examining whether AI chips brought into the country by a unit of Megaspeed were subsequently shipped overseas. The trade ministry said Megaspeed unit Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd is a tenant at data centres in Malaysia and brings in its own servers and AI chips for its operations.

Megaspeed is under scrutiny following reports that its former chief executive officer Alice Huang allegedly helped Chinese technology companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips.

stories.title: Malaysia 'has never cleared' Megaspeed and Speedmatrix
stories.summary: Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry explicitly denied approving Singapore-based Megaspeed International or its local affiliate Speedmatrix, deepening the controversy around alleged diversion of Nvidia chips. The statement comes as U.S. authorities investigate whether millions of dollars worth of GPUs were improperly routed through Malaysian entities.
stories.why_it_matters: This official denial raises the stakes for Malaysia's data center credibility: if MITI never cleared these firms, how did they operate and who enabled their GPU flows? The scandal now threatens to trigger tighter scrutiny of all Malaysian data center operators, potentially slowing investment approvals and forcing foreign hyperscalers to re-verify their local partners' legitimacy.
stories.title_zh: 马来西亚称"从未批准"Megaspeed和Speedmatrix
stories.summary_zh: 马来西亚投资、贸易及工业部（MITI）明确否认批准总部位于新加坡的Megaspeed International或其本地关联公司Speedmatrix，加剧了围绕 alleged Nvidia芯片转移争议的复杂性。该声明发布之际，美国当局正在调查价值数百万美元的GPU是否通过马来西亚实体被不当转移。
stories.why_zh: 这一官方否认提高了马来西亚数据中心信誉的风险：如果MITI从未批准这些公司，它们如何运作，谁促成了其GPU流动？该丑闻现在可能触发对所有马来西亚数据中心运营商的更严格审查，潜在减缓投资审批，并迫使外国hyperscale重新核实其本地合作伙伴的合法性。
stories.content:
The Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (MITI) in a statement last Friday has categorically stated that it “never cleared Singapore-based Megaspeed International Pte Ltd or its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd.”

Megaspeed and Speedmatrix are at the center of an alleged national security scandal at Nvidia. They are alleged to have channelled millons of dollars worth of restricted Nvidia high end chips to China.

MITI said Speedmatrix is a tenant at data centers in Malaysia and brings its own servers and AI chips into Malaysia for its operations. “Bringing AI chips into Malaysia does not currently require a permit or a licence,” the ministry clarified.

It further said any verification visits it carried out at the facilities “are part of its regular monitoring of the data centre sector, and should not be taken to mean that a company has been cleared. Any suggestion otherwise is inaccurate.”

MITI’s investigation involved checking whether re-exports occurred and whether they complied with Malaysian law. It was working with the Royal Malaysian Customs Department to determine whether any of the chips brought into Malaysia have since been reexported to other countries, and whether such reexports were carried out in accordance with the law.

It added that it would conduct independent checks under Malaysian law while cooperating with Singapore and US authorities on further measures to strengthen controls where necessary.

MITI said while Malaysia does not enforce unilateral export controls imposed by other countries, all companies operating in Malaysia are expected to take such controls into account in their international business.

“Malaysia welcomes investment in data centers and technology, but will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls. The government will take stern action against any company found to have broken Malaysian law.”

Since July 2025, anyone seeking to export, reexport, transship or transit high performance US AI chips from or through Malaysia must first obtain a permit from MITI under the Strategic Trade Act 2010. Giving false information to Customs about such goods is also a serious offence under the Customs Act 1967.

MITI stated it had not established wrongdoing on the part of Megaspeed and Speedmatrix \[so far\].

stories.title_zh: EcoWorld与Johor投资部门探索为数据中心和工业园区提供绿色公用事业供应
stories.summary_zh: 马来西亚房地产开发商EcoWorld已与柔佛州投资工具Permodalan Darul Ta'zim（PDT）合作，探索为该州数据中心和工业园区提供可再生能源（RE）和再生水。该合作针对在Iskandar Malaysia走廊扩张的hyperscale运营商的可持续性要求。
stories.why_zh: 该合作揭示了柔佛 emerging 的差异化策略：将土地、可再生能源和水回收打包为 integrated 价值主张，而非仅在成本套利上竞争。对评估柔佛与巴淡岛或曼谷的hyperscale而言，EcoWorld-PDT的公用事业捆绑减少了多供应商可持续性合规的复杂性；对本地竞争对手而言，这提高了门槛——未来的数据中心土地项目现在必须包含可信的绿色公用事业路线图，否则 risk 被具有净零承诺的运营商 bypass。
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 16): Eco World Development Group Bhd (KL:ECOWLD) has teamed up with the Johor state government’s investment arm Permodalan Darul Ta’zim Sdn Bhd (PDT) to explore supplying renewable energy (RE) and reclaimed water to data centres and industrial parks in the state.

Under a collaboration agreement signed between the two parties, PDT will explore facilitating the supply of green utilities through its subsidiaries, PDT Energy Sdn Bhd (PDTEN) and Johor Special Water Sdn Bhd (JSW), to EcoWorld’s industrial and data centre customers as an integrated offering.

The proposed arrangement is subject to further discussions on pricing and commercial terms, which will be set out in definitive supply agreements.

EcoWorld, meanwhile, will promote the green utility offerings to its network of Green Consumers and provide PDT’s subsidiaries with relevant information on prospective off-takers, including anticipated electricity load profiles, demand forecasts and project timelines, subject to the necessary consent, the property developer said in a statement on Monday.

The collaboration is aimed at strengthening Johor’s appeal as an investment destination by supporting the growing demand for sustainable utilities among industrial players and data centre operators.

Johor recorded RM110 billion in approved investments in 2025, the highest among all Malaysian states, while emerging as a key regional hub for data centre investments.

“The collaboration agreement supports the state’s aims to drive green investments and technology adoption while encouraging industries to improve energy efficiency and optimise the use of water resources,” said EcoWorld.

“Together, these efforts will help sustain Johor’s momentum in high-value economic growth, while ensuring EcoWorld’s industrial projects continue to be supported by reliable, efficient and sustainable utilities,” the group added.

At the time of writing on Monday, EcoWorld’s share price was down four sen or 2.21% at RM1.77, valuing the group at RM5.73 billion.

stories.title: SK Hynix plans chip testing hub to boost global competitiveness of smaller South Korean players
stories.summary: SK Hynix unveiled plans for a 874.6 billion won Trinity Fab testing facility scheduled to open in May 2027, designed to serve smaller South Korean semiconductor companies with advanced packaging and verification capabilities. The hub aims to reduce reliance on foreign testing infrastructure and level the playing field for domestic players competing against integrated global giants.
stories.why_it_matters: By opening its testing infrastructure to smaller Korean chip firms, SK Hynix is effectively building a national semiconductor ecosystem defense line: domestic fabless and memory companies gain faster iteration cycles and lower costs without sending proprietary designs to overseas test houses in Taiwan or China. For the broader APAC foundry landscape, this reduces captive business for independent testing houses like ASE or Amkor while potentially accelerating Korea's bid to replicate Taiwan's vertically integrated supply chain advantages.
stories.title_zh: SK Hynix计划建设芯片测试中心以提升韩国小型企业全球竞争力
stories.summary_zh: SK Hynix公布了8746亿韩元的Trinity Fab测试设施计划，定于2027年5月开业，旨在为韩国较小的半导体公司提供先进封装和验证能力。该hub旨在减少对外国测试基础设施的依赖，并为与 integrated 全球巨头竞争的 domestic players 创造公平竞争环境。
stories.why_zh: 通过向较小的韩国芯片公司开放其测试基础设施，SK Hynix实际上正在建设一条国家半导体生态系统防线：domestic fabless和memory公司获得更快的迭代周期和更低的成本，而无需将专有设计送往台湾或中国的海外测试厂。对更广泛的APAC foundry格局而言，这减少了ASE或Amkor等独立测试厂的 captive 业务，同时可能加速韩国复制台湾垂直整合供应链优势的 bid。
stories.content:
The 874.6 billion won Trinity Fab facility is set to open in May 2027

SK HYNIX plans to open a semiconductor testing facility in 2027 in partnership with the South Korean government, angling to boost the global competitiveness of the country’s smaller chip equipment makers.

The 874.6 billion won (US$654 million) facility is being built inside the sprawling Yongin Semiconductor Cluster, which is under construction south of Seoul, SK Hynix said in a statement on Monday (Nov 16).

The Trinity Fab facility will open in May with equipment that small and medium-sized suppliers can use to conduct final performance and yield validation before their products are deployed in commercial chipmaking lines, it said.

SK Hynix and homegrown rival Samsung Electronics have enjoyed an unprecedented run-up in prices because of a chip scarcity that has squeezed industries from autos to smartphones.

The company is working with the South Korean government to eliminate a critical hurdle in the country’s supply chain that has required access to expensive manufacturing infrastructure.

The facility is being jointly financed by SK Hynix, the central government and local authorities, the company said.

It will house about 50 pieces of equipment for lithography, etching, deposition, cleaning and measurement, allowing suppliers to test products on 12-inch wafers under conditions resembling those of commercial chip production.

The initiative aims to address a longstanding bottleneck for South Korea’s semiconductor supply chain.

Smaller materials and equipment makers often face steep costs and lengthy delays in securing access to production-scale testing facilities, making it difficult to demonstrate that their technologies meet the stringent performance and yield requirements of advanced chip manufacturing.

Unlike conventional research laboratories and pilot lines, Trinity Fab will be the world’s first open-access testing facility specifically designed to validate commercial manufacturing readiness for mass production, according to SK Hynix.

An independent non-profit foundation will operate the centre to safeguard participants’ intellectual property.

In August, SK Hynix said it would spend US$38 billion to expand its local chipmaking facilities, including a new Dram manufacturing facility in Yongin and a Nand fabrication plant in Cheongju.

The move, covering both dynamic memory for the lowest latency and solid-state storage for fast access to greater quantities of data, is in response to growing demand for memory in the artificial intelligence era, the company said at the time. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: The next AI play: Applications and biotech
stories.summary: AFTER years of investor enthusiasm for semiconductor manufacturers, data centre operators and technology giants pouring billions into artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, investors are now scrutinising how the massive spending will translate into sustainable earnings and cash flow. ...

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: 下一个AI投资方向：应用和生物科技
stories.content:
This article first appeared in Capital, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on November 9, 2026 - November 15, 2026

AFTER years of investor enthusiasm for semiconductor manufacturers, data centre operators and technology giants pouring billions into artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, investors are now scrutinising how the massive spending will translate into sustainable earnings and cash flow.

As attention turns to identifying the next beneficiaries of the AI cycle, Franklin Equity head of Asia-Pacific client portfolio management William Chang tells The Edge that businesses putting AI to practical use represent a compelling, underappreciated segment of the investment landscape.

“Some of the products that have been released lately that have been getting a lot of downloads are examples of the way that companies are using AI to grow their new software offerings,” he says, pointing to enterprise AI applications, AI-enabled software platforms and consumer applications, where businesses are developing new products and services as the technology becomes more widely adopted.

“When we look at the use of AI, we think that is a much bigger opportunity.”

Chang notes that investors are paying much closer attention to the quality of earnings reported by US tech giants, particularly whether their massive AI investments are generating adequate returns. Citing Meta as an example of a company whose AI-related products have drawn considerable interest, he says market expectations continue to rise.

“The bar is continually reset higher and higher. We think investors are going to continue to be more particular about what’s coming through in their earnings results and whether or not the billions of dollars of investment that they’re making is able to generate an acceptable return,” he adds.

Cumulative AI infrastructure expenditure is estimated to reach US$9 trillion to US$10 trillion through the early 2030s, while global spending next year alone could amount to US$1.2 trillion to US$1.3 trillion.

Chang believes investors are increasingly shifting their focus from ambitious spending plans and growth projections to actual financial performance. While he remains constructive on global AI spending over the next two to three years, he anticipates near-term volatility arising from US political developments affecting AI model training and concerns about the industry’s growing electricity consumption. “It’s not going to be a straight line up,” he surmises.

For Malaysian investors, a key consideration is whether opportunities in AI extend beyond the semiconductor, construction, utility and data centre-related counters that have dominated attention on Bursa Malaysia. After all, Malaysia’s semiconductor ecosystem and expanding role as a regional data centre hub have positioned it to benefit from the infrastructure-building phase of the AI boom.

While Chang believes the country remains well placed to continue participating in this build-out, he suggests investors consider a broader range of opportunities across the AI value chain, including companies listed overseas. “Certainly, there are opportunities within Malaysia itself, but the growth and rise of AI is global in nature. A lot of these companies are based out of the US but there’re also a lot of companies, particularly the foundries, that are based out of Asia,” he says.

Beyond mainstream technology hardware and software, Chang sees opportunities in biotechnology, where AI is driving innovation in drug discovery, while rising acquisition interest from major pharmaceutical companies provides another potential valuation catalyst.

Notable listed players leveraging AI in drug development are Recursion Pharmaceuticals and Schrödinger (Nasdaq: SDGR), as well as Hong Kong-listed Insilico Medicine.

For context, the biotech sector endured a prolonged downturn following its pandemic-era boom in 2021, as rising interest rates, tighter funding conditions and regulatory uncertainty weighed on valuations and investor sentiment, particularly among smaller drug developers. The sector began recovering in the latter half of 2025, supported by easing monetary conditions and renewed mergers and acquisitions (M&A).

US biotechnology companies such as Fate Therapeutics, Editas Medicine and Sangamo Therapeutics were among those affected and forced to reduce headcount and scale back development programmes. The segment began staging a recovery in late 2025, driven by renewed fundraising, advances in drug development and increasing M&A as major pharmaceutical companies seek to replenish their pipelines ahead of upcoming patent expirations.

Chang sees AI-driven innovation as one of the major factors behind renewed investor interest in biotechnology. “We are seeing a lot of the innovation taking place in AI trickle into the biotech space, and we think that’s likely to continue,” he predicts.

To illustrate the pace of innovation, Chang notes that the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved an average of 45 novel drugs annually over the past decade. “\[As of quite recently,\] the agency had already approved 46, with nearly three months remaining in the year,” he says.

Apart from AI-driven innovation, he highlights the pickup in M&A as another catalyst for the biotechnology sector’s recovery.

According to healthcare research firm IQVIA, the global biopharmaceutical M&A deal value surged 133% year on year to US$133 billion in 2025,before reaching US$130 billion in the first six months of 2026.

“While we’re constructive on the space, stock selection remains critical, particularly around innovative companies. We want to make sure they have differentiated collectible assets and they have a strong management team and improving fundamentals that can continue to generate returns for investors,” Chang emphasises.

stories.title: AI data centre demand drives chip shortage, raises costs for Indian automakers
stories.summary: Growing demand from AI data centres is tightening global chip supplies, leading to increased procurement costs for Indian automakers. Companies like Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles and Mahindra & Mahindra have reported paying higher prices to secure essential semiconductor components.
stories.title_zh: AI data centre需求推动chip短缺，抬高印度汽车制造商成本
stories.content:
Demand from artificial intelligence (AI) data centres is tightening global chip supplies, pushing up procurement costs for Indian automakers.This trend is also raising concerns over potential production disruptions across the industry.Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles (TMPV) Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Shailesh Chandra acknowledged the company was paying higher prices to secure semiconductor and electronic components. TMPV has managed to avoid production disruptions so far, Chandra said during the company’s September-quarter earnings call. Securing supplies had come at a premium, he added.Mahindra & Mahindra (M&M) flagged similar concerns during its March quarter 2025-26 (Q4FY26) earnings call in May. Rajesh Jejurikar, executive director and CEO (auto and farm sector) at M&M, warned that growing demand for memory chips from AI applications could prolong supply constraints for automakers. The issue would not go away for a while, Jejurikar stated.M&M was aggressively purchasing memory chips in the aftermarket to build inventories and safeguard production, despite higher procurement costs, Jejurikar said. The shortage is not restricted to electric vehicles (EVs), as memory chips are used in infotainment systems and other electronic components across both conventional and electric models, M&M had indicated earlier.Electric two-wheeler (E2W) maker Ather Energy also flagged persistent cost pressures. During its October earnings call, CEO Tarun Mehta said memory-chip prices had remained elevated despite earlier expectations of moderation. Mehta noted there was no near-term solution for the complicated and expensive memories.Global semiconductor manufacturers are echoing these concerns. Nexperia interim CEO Stefan Tilger told Reuters on November 10 at the Electronica trade fair in Munich that the Dutch chipmaker was “totally oversubscribed”. Suppliers were diverting manufacturing capacity towards AI data centres and away from conventional semiconductors used in automobiles and industrial equipment, Tilger added.STMicroelectronics CEO Jean-Marc Chery also warned that semiconductor foundries and chip-packaging companies were increasingly shifting resources away from mainstream automotive and industrial applications. This shift is creating supply-chain bottlenecks, Chery stated.Research firms are forecasting significant price increases. S&P Global Mobility forecasts new automotive Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM) contract prices could rise by 70-100 per cent in 2026 compared with 2025. The research firm expects supplies to remain constrained through 2027. Automakers willing to pay higher prices should generally be able to secure the volumes they require, S&P Global Mobility noted.Counterpoint Research warned in an August report that shortages of Double Data Rate 4 (DDR4) and Low-Power Double Data Rate 4 (LPDDR4) memory chips for automakers could persist beyond 2027. Automakers are responding by entering into long-term supply agreements, Counterpoint Research said. They are also shifting towards newer memory technologies such as DDR5, the firm added.The Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA) President Sai Giridhar cited shortages of specialised chips for batteries and electronic systems as a factor affecting EV availability in India. Some customers face waiting periods of up to eight months, Giridhar noted.FADA's November 6 retail report stated EV registrations reached a record 3.55 lakh units in October, up 44.88 per cent year-on-year. Demand had outstripped supply, with vehicle availability emerging as the principal constraint on further growth, Giridhar said.

- AI & Compute Infrastructure
- 3 min Read

# AI data centre demand drives chip shortage, raises costs for Indian automakers

Growing demand from AI data centres is tightening global chip supplies, leading to increased procurement costs for Indian automakers. Companies like Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles and Mahindra & Mahindra have reported paying higher prices to secure essential semiconductor components.

- Published On Nov 16, 2026 at 10:15 AM IST

## Highlights

- AI data centre demand is tightening global chip supplies.
- Indian automakers face higher procurement costs for semiconductors.
- Memory chip prices remain elevated, with supply constraints expected through 2027.
- Automakers are adopting long-term agreements and newer memory technologies.

stories.title: Thailand draws on AWS to expand data centers after rules tightening
stories.summary: Thai officials met with Amazon Web Services to discuss expanding its cloud infrastructure footprint in Thailand, pairing the engagement with new government promises of streamlined approvals and clean energy access. The outreach comes paradoxically after Bangkok tightened data center regulations to emphasize sustainability requirements.
stories.why_it_matters: Thailand is threading a needle: tighter rules could deter investors, so the government is simultaneously rolling out red-carpet mechanisms—one-stop services, faster approvals, green procurement—to keep hyperscalers like AWS committed. For AWS, the dual signals mean negotiating favorable terms while meeting new sustainability benchmarks; for regional rivals Singapore and Malaysia, it signals Thailand's determination not to be bypassed in the AI infrastructure race.
stories.title_zh: 泰国在规则收紧后携手AWS扩展数据中心
stories.summary_zh: 泰国官员与Amazon Web Services（AWS）会面，讨论扩大其在泰国的cloud infrastructure布局，同时政府承诺简化审批流程并提供清洁能源获取渠道。此次接触颇具矛盾性地发生在曼谷收紧数据中心法规以强调可持续性要求之后。
stories.why_zh: 泰国正在走钢丝：更严格的规则可能 deter 投资者，因此政府同时推出贵宾机制——一站式服务、更快审批、绿色采购——以保持AWS等hyperscale的承诺。对AWS而言，双重信号意味着在满足新可持续性基准的同时谈判有利条款；对区域竞争对手新加坡和马来西亚而言，这 signal 泰国决心不在AI基础设施竞赛中被 bypass。
stories.content:
The Anutin government last Thursday discussed with Amazon Web Services (AWS) to expand its data centers in Thailand, according to local publication <u>Banmuang.</u>  The Thai government also outlined plans for a data center one-stop service, faster investment approvals, clean energy procurement and workforce development.

This came following Thailand’s tightening of data center rules to chart a sustainable growth path for its booming data center industry.

To support the growth of data centers, AWS affirmed its commitment to clean energy, including direct PPA and air cooling technology. The tech giant has previously pledged to invest more than US$ 5 billion over 15 years in Thailand. The first phase of the data center project worth more than 24,800 million baht and the AWS Asia Pacific (Thailand) Region have been previously launched.

At the same time, AWS continues to develop the skills of the Thai digital workforce through partnerships with universities and educational institutions.

The proposed Data Center One Stop Service seeks to promote the Board of Investment’s Thailand Fast Pass Service measures while at the same time reducing the approval and permitting processes in order to create a conducive environment for investment.

Besides Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnwirakul, executives of the Board of Investment (BOI) and the Office of the National Economic and Social Development Council (NESDC) were also present at the discussion.

stories.title: Thai GDP growth rebounds as AI drives investments, exports
stories.summary: Thailand's economic growth accelerated as AI-related investments, data center construction, and advanced electronics exports contributed significantly to GDP recovery. The surge reflects Bangkok's partial success in repositioning the economy toward digital infrastructure and high-value manufacturing after prolonged reliance on tourism and traditional industries.
stories.why_it_matters: Thailand's GDP rebound validates the government's bet that data center and AI infrastructure investments can diversify growth beyond tourism volatility, but the composition matters: if AI-driven capital inflows concentrate in land and power deals rather than skills and R&D, the boom becomes extractive rather than transformative. For regional competitors, Thailand's momentum signals that second-tier ASEAN markets can capture meaningful AI infrastructure spend if they package incentives with workforce development; for Thai citizens, the test is whether GDP growth translates to employment quality, not just construction jobs and electricity demand spikes.

stories.title_zh: 泰国GDP增长反弹，AI推动投资和出口
stories.summary_zh: 泰国经济增长加速，因为AI相关投资、数据中心建设和先进电子产品出口对GDP复苏做出了重大贡献。该 surge 反映了曼谷在长期依赖旅游业和传统产业后，向数字基础设施和高价值制造业 repositioning 经济的部分成功。
stories.why_zh: 泰国的GDP反弹验证了政府的赌注，即数据中心和AI基础设施投资可以使增长超越旅游业波动而多元化，但构成很重要：如果AI驱动的资本流入集中在土地和电力交易而非技能和研发，繁荣将变成 extractive 而非变革性的。对区域竞争对手而言，泰国的 momentum signal 表明，如果二线东盟市场将激励措施与劳动力发展相结合，就能 capture 有意义的AI基础设施支出；对泰国公民而言，考验在于GDP增长是否转化为就业质量，而不仅仅是 construction 工作和电力需求 spike。
stories.content:
The country attracts a surge in investment tied to AI, data centres and advanced electronics

THAILAND shed its place as South-east Asia’s slowest-growing major economy in the third quarter, with the artificial-intelligence boom powering exports while masking persistent weakness in household spending and tourism.

Gross domestic product in the three months through September rose 2.9 per cent from a year earlier, the National Economic and Social Development Council said on Monday. That was below the 3.1 per cent median estimate in a Bloomberg survey. Second-quarter growth was restated at 2.4 per cent from 1.9 per cent.

The pickup partly reflected a favourable comparison with a year earlier, when US tariffs and a border conflict with Cambodia disrupted trade. But it also showed the growing impact of the global AI investment cycle on Thailand, where electronics exports and private investment have surged.

Investment growth accelerated to 11.8 per cent in the third quarter, while exports jumped 18.3 per cent, the council said. Household consumption ticked up just 2.5 per cent, while government spending shrank 1.6 per cent.

The economic data put Thailand ahead of the Philippines, which expanded 2.1 per cent in the quarter. The country still trailed most regional peers, with Vietnam growing almost 10 per cent and Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia all expanding more than 5 per cent.

Growth above 3 per cent has become unusual for Thailand, an aging tiger economy constrained by high household debt and limited fiscal room.

The country last grew more than 3 per cent in a quarter in early 2025 and hasn’t recorded annual growth above that level since 2018.

The stronger performance comes during a period of unusual political stability.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul leads one of Thailand’s strongest governing coalitions in decades, giving his administration more room to pursue investment and economic policies even with a no-confidence vote looming next month and street protests simmering.

Thailand has also attracted a surge in investment tied to AI, data centres and advanced electronics, while foreign investors have returned to its bonds and stocks. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Malaysia mulls laws to monitor data center chips movement: Minister
stories.summary: Malaysian Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani revealed plans for legislation that would mandate data center operators to disclose facility locations, actual operators, and detailed GPU import records to authorities. The proposed law represents Kuala Lumpur's most direct response yet to concerns about chip diversion and national security vulnerabilities in its booming data center sector.
stories.why_it_matters: If enacted, this law would give Malaysian regulators unprecedented visibility into the black box of GPU supply chains, potentially catching unauthorized chip movements before they become international scandals. However, hyperscale operators and colocation providers may resist the transparency burden, especially if disclosures reveal competitive sensitivities about customer identities and deployment timelines; the compliance friction could slow Malaysia's current investment boom if rival jurisdictions offer lighter oversight.
stories.title_zh: 马来西亚部长：考虑立法监控数据中心芯片流动
stories.summary_zh: 马来西亚贸易及工业部长Johari Abdul Ghani透露了立法计划，将强制数据中心运营商向当局披露设施位置、实际运营商及详细的GPU进口记录。该拟议法律代表了吉隆坡对其蓬勃发展的数据中心行业中芯片转移和国家安全漏洞担忧的最直接回应。
stories.why_zh: 如果 enacted，该法律将使马来西亚监管机构前所未有地了解GPU供应链的黑箱，潜在在国际丑闻发生前发现未经授权的芯片流动。然而，hyperscale运营商和colocation提供商可能抵制这种透明度负担，特别是如果披露揭示了关于客户身份和部署时间线的竞争敏感性；如果 rival 司法管辖区提供更宽松的监管，合规摩擦可能减缓马来西亚当前的投资热潮。
stories.content:
Malaysia is considering a new law that would compel data centers to reveal to the government their facilities’ operators and locations, as well as the details of their graphics processing units (GPUs) imports, Reuters reported last week citing Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani.

This followed the fallout from Nvidia CEO’s Jensen Huang’s alleged ties with a suspected Chinese spy and the ensuing greater scrutiny on the country’s GPU movement through its data centers. Malaysia had last year imposed export controls on the movement of US-origin advanced AI chips following pressure from the US. The US had alleged that some data centers in Malaysia were used to circumvent US’ restrictions on the use of the chips by China.

Johari added that Malaysia wanted to ensure that US-restricted chips that were imported into the country were used domestically instead of being re-exported to a third country.

On Speedmatrix, the Malaysian unit of Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed International Pte Ltd, that had been alleged to be used to channel AI chips to China, Johari reportedly said: “If… they buy the GPUs for their own use in the data centres, then I cannot see what law that we need to use (to investigate them).”

On its website, Megaspeed through its chairman and CEO, James Tan Yong Pong, said in a statement published last Thursday that it took “its compliance obligations under U.S. export control laws extremely seriously.”

“Compliance is a fundamental priority for the company, and Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government. Megaspeed has cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) and stands ready to cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority.”

The firm added that it had hired a leading U.S. law firm to lead a comprehensive census of its GPUs independently to verify its export control compliance practices.

stories.title: What's behind a data centre's asset valuation and business value?
stories.summary: Singapore's restrictive land and power policies have created a supply-constrained market where hybrid data center assets—combining colocation and hyperscale characteristics—command premium valuations and resilient returns. The city-state's regulatory environment effectively insulates incumbent operators from oversupply risks plaguing more permissive regional markets.
stories.why_it_matters: Singapore's artificial scarcity model is becoming a template for disciplined data center economics: investors and operators who secured capacity before the moratorium now enjoy pricing power that newer markets like Johor or Bangkok cannot replicate quickly. For capital allocators, this validates paying higher entry multiples for Singapore assets; for governments across ASEAN, it presents a tension—liberalize to attract volume, or restrict to protect returns and grid stability, with Singapore having clearly chosen the latter path.

stories.summary_zh: 新加坡严格的土地和电力政策创造了一个供应受限的市场，其中结合colocation和hyperscale特性的hybrid数据中心资产享有premium估值和 resilient 回报。该城邦的监管环境有效保护了现有运营商免受困扰更宽松区域市场的 oversupply 风险。

stories.content:
Singapore is emerging as a haven for the hybrid assets, where constrained supply keeps pricing firm and returns high

\[SINGAPORE\] High valuations, rapidly mounting investments and the debt required to finance them are bringing data centre assets under scrutiny.

As investors wrangle with a boom-to-bust scenario and growing backlash against build-out, Singapore is emerging as a data centre haven where constrained supply keeps pricing firm and returns high.

Understanding the value and valuation of data centres will help investors and developers allocate their investments more effectively.

Far more than the industrial real estate they are housed in, data centres are crucial infrastructure underpinning all digital services in modern economies. One only has to look at Microsoft’s recent Outlook outage to understand the devastation that server downtime can wreak on everyday activity and global business.

Sending an e-mail, paying a bill, booking a private-hire ride, shopping online – these now-basic activities, and most other types of commerce today, rely on computing resources to process, store and exchange information.

Because individual and payment data is stored in data centres using advanced database systems, physical security, cybersecurity and operational reliability are central to data centre design.

Tech giants such as Meta, Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS) build their own AI-focused data centre campuses to train large language models (LLMs), used to produce inference and generative outputs.

Nor do data centres operate in isolation. Servers connect through high-speed fibre-optic cables to servers in other data centres, creating virtual networks across multi-cloud environments. These interconnected resources distribute data and support application deliveries across different environments.

## Not just real estate

Crucially, data centres require a reliable electricity supply, backed up by redundancy via batteries and standby generators.

Servers and computers densely packed in a data centre also generate intense heat, which must be cooled with air or liquid cooling systems, including multiple chillers and cooling towers, to prevent overheating.

Compared with conventional industrial buildings, data centres require substantial capital investment in backup power and cooling infrastructure to sustain continuous operations. According to Cushman and Wakefield’s *Asia Pacific Data Centre Construction Cost Guide 2026*, these systems account for an estimated 44 per cent of total development costs, while the building shell and land account for about 24 per cent.

The substantial investment required in mechanical, electrical and water systems leads some investors to view data centres as infrastructure assets, comparable to seaports, rather than conventional real estate.

Since lifting a three-year moratorium on new data centre projects in 2022, Singapore has pushed for “sustainable” data centres, giving out licences subject to strict energy standards. It has also announced plans to build a low-carbon data centre park on Jurong Island with up to 700 megawatts (MW) of capacity.

Licences for building new large-scale data centres in Singapore are allocated through competitive calls.

The Data Centre Call for Application (DC-CFA) framework is jointly administered by the Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA).

In August, four operators – Digital Realty, Equinix, Keppel Data Centres and ST Telemedia Global Data Centres – were each allocated 50 MW of new capacity, subject to strict green energy standards.

In such a supply-constrained market, data centre pricing is likely to hold firm against a global backdrop of increasing supply and uncertain returns.

Data centre operators are also expected to pay premiums for new data centre licences here.

## Valuations and the business model

Long leases provide relatively predictable rental income that supports the purchase price, but valuation must reflect the lease terms, income risks and the landlord’s expenditure obligations.

Institutional investors will prefer a more complex discounted cash flow method to determine investment feasibility. However, valuers will apply three conventional valuation methods to determine the value of a typical co-location data centre: direct comparison, cost and income.

For a hypothetical co-location data centre with capacity of 5 MW, and based on an estimated total construction costs of S$23,270 per kilowatt (kW), the total construction costs for the building shell, standby power generators, cooling systems and land (excluding servers and IT equipment) are estimated at S$116.4 million, going by Cushman & Wakefield’s 2026 cost guide.

By direct comparison against transactions of two data centres sold in Japan in November 2025 and March 2026 for an average price of S$31.6 million per MW, according to *CBRE’s 2026 Asia Pacific Data Centre Trends & Outlook*, the 5 MW co-location data centre would be valued at S$158.1 million.

Using the income method, based on a monthly rent of S$400 per kW at a 95 per cent occupancy rate, and outgoing expenses of 35 per cent, we derive a net rental income of S$14.8 million per year for the co-location data centre space (without servers).

Using a discount rate of 6.5 per cent per annum, the estimated value of the 5 MW co-location data centre with a 30-year lease is about S$197 million.

The estimated value based on the income method is much higher than the values estimated using the contractor’s cost and direct sale comparison methods.

Based on the same net rental income, yields are estimated at around 12.7 per cent and 8.74 per cent for the values estimated, using the contractor’s cost method and past average transaction prices, respectively.

The differential yields also imply that investors will pay higher prices for data centre assets in Singapore relative to construction costs.

Aside from the valuations, investors must also conduct careful due diligence and understand the assets they purchase, including ownership rights of the IT servers and equipment and which equipment count as fixtures.

Mechanical and electrical standby generators, cooling plants and systems are fixed to the data centre’s shell and structure which belong to data centre owners; the fixtures thus belong to the data centre owners and cannot be removed.

Graphics processing units packed in server racks and other IT equipment are usually fixed and connected to the raised-floor system in data centres for security and operational reasons.

In co-location data centres, these servers and IT equipment are installed and owned by tenants; they are considered tenants’ fixtures and are removable on lease expiry. However, in managed hosting service data centers, operators install, own, and manage those server systems for their tenants and users.

In Singapore, the inelastic supply of data centres due to power supply constraints will hold up prices. Still, one factor that can affect value is the technological depreciation of servers and equipment, which are not usually owned by data centre asset owners.

Servers and other IT equipment generally have shorter economic lives than the building shell, mechanical and electrical infrastructure, and cooling plants. Technological advances accelerate obsolescence, and data centre investors and tenants must understand the useful life and set aside sufficient funds to account for depreciation.

Even when the equipment remains the tenants’ fixtures and is not included in the acquisition, investors who acquire the property interest are still entitled to existing leases that generate steady long-term cash flows.

Yet, tenants are responsible for replacing and upgrading servers and equipment, and may need to set aside funds for such upgrades and replacements.

Businesses with limited resources can procure on-demand cloud computing resources directly from hyperscale providers such as AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure, rather than managing their own server systems.

**Sing Tien Foo is provost’s chair professor, and Alice Christudason is associate professor at the Department of Real Estate, Business School, National University of Singapore. stories.title: Firmus plans $4.4b private raise but up-front Nvidia, Meta payments key
stories.summary: Australian data center developer Firmus is targeting a $4.4 billion private capital raise, with the success of the fundraising contingent on securing advance payment commitments from anchor tenants Nvidia and Meta for its planned facilities. The structure reflects the immense capital intensity of modern AI-optimized data centers and the shift toward tenant-backed financing models.
stories.why_it_matters: Firmus's financing architecture reveals how the AI data center buildout is restructuring capital markets: without pre-commitments from hyperscalers with investment-grade credit, even promising developers cannot attract institutional capital at scale. For Nvidia and Meta, the upfront payment demands create a strategic bind—lock in capacity early to secure GPU deployment slots, or preserve capital flexibility and risk supply constraints; their choices will determine which regional developers survive the current construction cycle.
stories.title_zh: Firmus计划44亿美元私募融资，但NVIDIA、Meta预付款是关键
stories.summary_zh: 澳大利亚数据中心开发商Firmus正瞄准44亿美元的私募融资，其成功取决于为计划中的设施从 anchor tenants Nvidia和Meta获得预付款承诺。该结构反映了现代AI优化数据中心的巨大资本密集度，以及向租户支持融资模式的转变。
stories.why_zh: Firmus的融资架构揭示了AI数据中心建设如何重构资本市场：没有来自投资级信用的hyperscale的预承诺，即使有前景的开发商也无法大规模吸引机构资本。对Nvidia和Meta而言，预付款需求创造了战略困境——提前锁定产能以确保GPU部署 slot，或保留资本灵活性并 risk 供应约束；它们的选择将决定哪些区域开发商能在当前建设周期中生存。
stories.content:
Firmus hopes to raise $US3 billion ($4.4 billion) privately by issuing new shares and debt and locking in prepayments from mega-customers including Nvidia and Meta, as the artificial intelligence infrastructure group seeks fresh funding following the spectacular collapse of its planned $44 billion ASX listing.

The pre-payment talks are the most advanced of Firmus’ raising plans and could facilitate about 12.5 per cent of the company’s contracts being paid up front to help fund yet-to-be-built AI and data centre capacity, three people with knowledge of the plan said on the condition of anonymity.
